title: Vasudeva Vipra
html:
A Brahmana of Kurma-kshetra

Among those whom Sri Chaitanya met on His journey through the South there is one whom almost no one knew before he met the Lord: the brahmana Vasudeva, Sri Vasudeva Vipra. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him a “noble brahmana” (dvija-mahashaya). He lived in the south of India, in utter poverty, lowly and unnoticed. Such a devotee — destitute, sick, in no way distinguished by worldly measures — ordinary people do not recognise; Mahaprabhu Himself revealed his glory to the world. In his brief summary of the Lord's pastimes Krishnadasa Kaviraja gives him a whole line:

“Then the Lord set out for the South. At Kurma-kshetra He delivered Vasudeva.” (CC, Madhya 1.102)1

The meeting took place at Kurma-kshetra (Kurmasthana), at the start of the Lord's journey through the South, in 1510, when Mahaprabhu was twenty-four.2 Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains in his “Anubhashya” that this is Kurmachalam, or Srikurmam, in Ganjam district, eight miles east of Chicacole Road station on the B. N. R. line — the most revered tirtha among Telugu speakers, where the Deity of Lord Kurma, the Tortoise avatara, resides. Today the station is called Srikakulam Road and the line the South Eastern Railway; the station lies in the state of Andhra Pradesh, while Ganjam district is in Orissa.

According to the same commentary, Sri Ramanuja came to Kurma-kshetra: Jagannatha carried him there, and Ramanuja, at first taking the Deity for a Shiva-linga, fasted until he recognised in Him Vishnu in the form of the Tortoise; then he opened His worship. Later the temple was under the supervision of the Sri Madhva Math, in the domain of the king of Vijayanagara.

Nothing more is known of Vasudeva's worldly life. The sources name neither his parents nor the days of his appearance and disappearance; nor are they in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. When he left this world is also unknown.

Leprosy

Vasudeva's whole body was eaten away by oozing leprosy (galat-kushtha). Krishnadasa Kaviraja relates:

“There was a noble brahmana named Vasudeva. His whole body was rotting with leprosy and swarming with worms. Whenever a worm slipped and fell from his body, he would pick it up and put it back in the same place.” (CC, Madhya 7.136–137)

The worms fed on his blood and pus, yet he did not drive them away: when one fell out, he lifted it and carefully put it back. The biographies marvel at this nature of his, and Kavi Karnapura in his drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” adds that he did it without the least disgust, as if his mind were absorbed in the Lord. There was neither worldly asceticism nor madness in this: so far did the humility and compassion of a devotee reach — even to the worms feeding on his body.3 People fled from the sight and stench of him while still far off; he himself would tell the Lord that even sinners ran away from him.

At Kurma's House

The Lord came to Kurma-kshetra and stayed in the house of a local brahmana named Kurma, whom He blessed.4 News of Him reached Vasudeva, and, sick as he was, he hurried in great impatience to Kurma's house. The “Charitamrita” says:

“At night he heard of the Gosani's arrival, and in the morning he came to Kurma's house to see Him. When he heard from Kurma that the Lord had gone, he fell to the ground unconscious with grief. He began to lament in many ways, and at that very moment the Lord came and embraced him.” (CC, Madhya 7.138–140)

The Lord is the Supersoul of all beings; though He had already gone far, He knew His devotee's grief and appeared before him. One of the biographies says plainly that the Lord came back; another says only that, having gone far, He appeared to Vasudeva and embraced him. What drew Him was the brahmana's heartfelt devotion.5

The Embrace

The Lord paid no regard to his leprosy. He embraced Vasudeva as one embraces the dearest — out of love for him as His devotee. The Lord is conquered by devotion alone; worldly merits and defects He does not take into account, nor does He look at any outward deformity or wretched condition of one wholly devoted to Him. Whoever longs for Him attains Him.

“At the Lord's touch his leprosy vanished together with his grief, and his body became beautiful and full of bliss.” (CC, Madhya 7.141)

He received the body of the most handsome of men.6 Amazed at such mercy, the brahmana remembered the words of Sudama — the poor brahmana, Krishna's childhood friend, whom the Lord had once met and embraced in just the same way in Dvaraka — and, holding the Lord's feet, glorified Him with a verse of the “Bhagavatam”:

“Who am I, a poor and sinful man, and who is Krishna, the abode of the goddess of fortune? Yet because I was born a brahmana, He embraced me in His arms!” (CC, Madhya 7.143; “Srimad-Bhagavatam” 10.81.16)7

The healing was neither the purpose of this meeting nor its chief wonder. The Lord embraced Vasudeva not to display His power but because He loves His devotee; the leprosy left of itself, at the touch of His body. Vasudeva himself had not asked to be healed — and, as we shall now see, he met his healing with fear rather than joy.

“Now Pride Will Arise in Me”

After offering the Lord many prayers, Vasudeva said:

“Hear me, O Merciful One: no jiva has this quality; it is found in You alone. Seeing me and smelling my stench, even the wretched flee from me; yet You touch someone like me. You are the independent Lord! But I was better off being lowly; now pride will arise in me.” (CC, Madhya 7.144–146)

Here is the heart of the whole story. What troubles Vasudeva now is not his illness but its cure: he fears that a beautiful body will bring honour, honour will bring pride, and he will fall. The proud lose the Lord's mercy and even the right to chant His names; that is why he prayed not for health but that he might not become proud.

The Order to Become an Acharya

The Lord answered him:

“You will never become proud. Chant the name ‘Krishna! Krishna!’ constantly. Teach about Krishna and deliver the jivas, and very soon Krishna will accept you as His own.” (CC, Madhya 7.147–148)

So the Lord found him fully worthy to be an acharya — a teacher who himself chants the name of Krishna without cease and instructs others in it. He assured Vasudeva that the beauty of his body would not bring him the conceit that usually comes with it. One of the biographies recalls this in its account of Kurma as well: the Lord embraced Vasudeva, made him most handsome, delivered him and, blessing him, assured him that his new body would not give rise to pride; and then He gave him as well the order to teach Krishna's name and so bring all jivas to deliverance.

A similar order the Lord gave on the same road to Kurma himself and to all the householders who received Him in their homes (Madhya 7.127–130). On these verses Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya”: to those who wish to give up everything for His service, Mahaprabhu says “stay at home” — that is, give up the pride of one “wholly given to bhajana,” chant the pure name with humility and preach it. To think, “I am the foremost of Vaishnavas; taking disciples would ruin my bhajana,” is the same pride; and whoever considers the books of Rupa, Sanatana, Jiva and Raghunatha Dasa, and the many disciples of Narottama, Madhva and Ramanuja, an obstacle to bhakti offends the selfless devotees. One who does the work of a guru with humility will not be swept away by the craving for fame. The words “stay at home” are not addressed to Vasudeva; but the thought is the same as in the order given to him: humility and preaching the name are the protection against pride.8

Another comment of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta (on Madhya 7.152) reveals the meaning of these orders. Sri Krishna Chaitanya brings jivas devoid of consciousness to consciousness; once awakened and turned to the service of Krishna, they in turn, as acharyas, awaken others. Thus, increasing the family of Achyuta and spreading the path of shrauta, Gaurasundara manifests the glory of His descent. Vasudeva is one of such acharyas, whom the Lord Himself awakened and sent forth.

Vasudevamrita-prada

“Having said this, the Lord disappeared, and the two brahmanas wept in each other's arms, remembering the Lord's qualities.” (CC, Madhya 7.149)

So the two brahmanas of Kurma-kshetra — the host in whose house the Lord had stayed and the leper whom He had embraced — were left alone together, weeping in separation from Him and remembering His mercy.9

Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls this pastime “Vasudeva-uddhara,” “the Deliverance of Vasudeva”; and from then on the Lord Himself had a new name:

“Thus I have told the story of Vasudeva's deliverance, through which the Lord received the name Vasudevamrita-prada, ‘the Giver of nectar to Vasudeva.’” (CC, Madhya 7.150)

Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura notes in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” that this name is among the “hundred names of Sri Chaitanya” composed by Sarvabhauma Bhattacharya. It also opens the whole seventh chapter of the Madhya-lila: the heading of the edition is an obeisance to “Vasudevamrita-prada,” and the first verse of the chapter praises the Lord whose heart melts with compassion, who “cured Vasudeva of leprosy, filled him with beauty and made him content in devotion” (Madhya 7.1). Concluding the account, Krishnadasa Kaviraja sums up: so began the Lord's journey — with His visit to Kurma and the deliverance of Vasudeva (7.151).

How Others Tell It

Other primary sources also preserve the story of Vasudeva, and each tells it in its own way.10

Murari Gupta writes that Vasudeva, “the best of brahmanas,” on seeing the Lord recognised Him as Krishna in rapture and began to dance; “Bhagavan embraced that brahmana, a leper and the best of great devotees, and he shone like gold” (“Kadacha” 3.14.17–18). To both His devotees, Vasudeva and Kurma, the Lord gave the order to lead people to devotion to Krishna — and vanished (3.14.19–20).

Kavi Karnapura in his mahakavya calls Vasudeva large-hearted, steadfast and honoured for his greatness. Hearing that the Lord had left Puri for the South, he — gravely ill, his body wasted like a reed and ceaselessly eaten away by leprosy — reached Kurma's house with great difficulty and himself asked Kurma about Mahaprabhu. Kurma replied: “Had you come only a moment earlier, you would have seen the Master right here.” Vasudeva cried out, “He has gone!” and fell unconscious; and then the Lord came back, embraced him and took away his swoon together with his leprosy. Bowing to the Lord in joy and sorrow, Vasudeva recited the same verse of Sudama and said: “Alas, this is not mercy — this is a punishment for me!” The Lord replied: “Do not lose heart: one who is free of selfishness will come to Me,” — and disappeared. Kurma too fell unconscious and lamented bitterly that he had not recognised God in his guest (“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” 12.106–117).

In the drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” the story of Vasudeva is told to Sarvabhauma and King Prataparudra by a brahmana returning from the South. No one had told the Lord about him — the Lord found him Himself and, as one embraces the closest of friends after long separation, held him tightly, just as he was. The brahmana uttered Sudama's verse, and at once his body became radiant and beautiful, “as it was by nature.” Then he said: “Lord! Why have You punished me so? While I was like that — diseased — I lived without sorrow and without agitation. But now, when honour comes to me, all the movements of the mind will rise again.” The Lord answered: “Brahmana! From now on your mind will turn to no external affairs, only to the remembrance of the Lord. So give up your anxiety.” Hearing this, the king said: “Bhattacharya! Truly He is Ishvara. Otherwise such compassion is impossible for a jiva — whereas even a great yogi can cure leprosy” (act 7, verse 3).

The words “this is a punishment for me” are no complaint against the Lord. They are the speech of humility, the same as in the “Charitamrita”: “I was better off being lowly.” What frightens Vasudeva is not health as such but the honour and pride that might draw him away from the Lord. And the king's words draw the same line as the whole story: a yogi too could remove leprosy, but to embrace a leper as a friend — only the Lord Himself.

Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” says that Vasudeva lay helpless on the outskirts of the town; learning that the Lord had stayed with Kurma, he came there fearlessly, and hearing that the Lord had left at dawn, he rolled on the ground, weeping: “Lord, protect me!” And the Lord, appearing at the threshold of the house, before Kurma's eyes embraced him again and again. Vasudeva's body became beautiful as that of Kama regaining his body; he cried: “Where am I, with a heart full of nothing but filth, and where are You, the sole abode of Kamala!” — and fell at the Lord's feet. The Lord raised him, instructed him and vanished like lightning; and those two, weeping in separation from Gaura, became honoured together with the townspeople (9.7–12).

Lochana Dasa in the Shesha-khanda writes that Vasudeva lived in the same village as Kurma, and that the Lord met them both in one place. By the sight of the Lord they became pure, recognised Gaurachandra as Krishna and fell at His feet; the Lord raised and embraced them both, asked them why they had come into the world and what they followed, and said: “In the Kali age the dharma is the sankirtana of Hari's name… Rejoice in singing the names and qualities [of the Lord]; dance, dance — let people be freed from bondage!” When the Lord hurried away, they forgot themselves. Of leprosy Lochana Dasa says nothing. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in his summary of this chapter, says that at Kurma-kshetra the Lord showed mercy to the brahmana Vasudeva and instructed him that the dharma of the Kali age is the holy name of Sri Hari alone, and from there came to Jiyada-Nrisimha. The lists of the journey run the same way: the deliverance of Vasudeva, and next Nrisimha of Jiyada, Simhachalam; so too in the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 8.3).

Finally, “The Harmonist” — Srila Bhaktisiddhanta's journal, in which a biography of the Lord was printed under his editorship (1928) — says that the Lord showed mercy to the brahmana Vasudeva, afflicted with malignant leprosy, freed him at once “from the diseases of body and mortality” and made him an acharya; for this the Lord became known as “Vasudevamrita-prada,” the One who gave Vasudeva nectar, that is, immortality.11 Immortality here is not a long life of the body but release from the cycle of birth and death — the nectar that the Lord's mercy bestows.

A Vaishnava's Body

Many years later, in Puri, the Lord was embracing Sanatana Gosvami, whose body was covered with sores, and Haridasa Thakura recalled Vasudeva:

“Vasudeva was a leper with oozing sores, his body full of worms, yet out of compassion You embraced him. By embracing him You made his body as beautiful as Kandarpa's. We cannot understand the waves of Your mercy.” (CC, Antya 4.189–190)

The Lord replied:

“A Vaishnava's body is never material. A devotee's body is transcendental (aprakrita), full of spirit and bliss (cid-ananda-maya).” (CC, Antya 4.191)

A devotee's body is not mundane; it is beyond this world, full of consciousness and bliss. One who lacks remembrance of Krishna sees it only from outside — sores, sickness, poverty — and does not see its spiritual nature. So the Lord Himself explained why He did not shrink from the sores of Vasudeva or of Sanatana.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains this verse in the “Anubhashya”: a Vaishnava's body is not a material body meant for enjoyment, like the body of a karmi, a jnani or one with other desires. A devotee's body is full of spiritual bliss, fit for the service of Krishna, and in it eternity, knowledge and bliss shine forth.

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, asks of him what his story teaches:

“Vasudeva Vipra! Take away my pride in the body: let there be no disgust in me, but abundant compassion for living beings.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 228)

Significance

Vasudeva Vipra shows how the Lord finds a devotee whom the world does not notice. Destitute, sick and shunned, he was a noble brahmana and the best of devotees, and Mahaprabhu Himself came to him, Himself embraced him and Himself made his glory known to all.

His story shows the compassion that the Lord and His devotees feel on seeing conditioned souls suffer. The Lord embraces one from whom everyone flees; Kurma and Vasudeva weep for Him in each other's arms; and Vasudeva, who fears only pride, the Lord makes an acharya and sends out to deliver others by the name of Krishna. For this the Lord received the name Vasudevamrita-prada.

Notes

  1. One of the biographies places this verse as an epigraph to the account of Vasudeva, numbered “1.103” — after the numbering of another edition; it also mentions the “Charitamrita”'s account of the worms (Madhya 7.136–137) but does not quote the verses themselves.
  2. The year and the Lord's age follow our chronology of the journey; the biographies give no dates. Where Vasudeva lived is told differently: Govinda-deva says on the outskirts of the town, Lochana Dasa — in the same village as Kurma.
  3. The sources are silent about the cause of his illness, and there is no ground for seeing it as a punishment for sins: the “Charitamrita” calls him a noble brahmana, Murari Gupta “the best of great devotees,” and the Lord Himself says that a Vaishnava's body is never mundane (Antya 4.191; see below).
  4. Kurma is a different person, the host in whose house the Lord stayed, and is not to be identified with Vasudeva. Nor should Vasudeva Vipra be confused with his namesakes: Vasudeva Datta, Vasudeva Ghosha, Vasudeva Sarvabhauma, Vasudeva Tirtha, Vasudeva nicknamed “Shiyal,” the brahmana Vasudeva of Koladvipa to whom Varaha appeared in the Satya-yuga, and still less with Vasudeva, the father of Krishna, or Vasudeva of the chatur-vyuha.
  5. According to the “Charitamrita,” the Lord “at that very moment came”; one of the biographies says He came back (so too Karnapura), another does not speak of a return. How the other primary sources tell the course of the meeting is described below.
  6. One of the biographies writes that he became “a healthy and handsome youth.” The “Charitamrita” says nothing of youth: his body became beautiful — in Haridasa Thakura's words, like that of the god of love (Antya 4.190).
  7. In the biographies the verse is numbered 10.81.15 and 10.89.16 (a misprint); the correct number is 10.81.16, as in the “Charitamrita” and the “Anubhashya.” The same verse is also quoted in Adi 17.78. Literally Sudama calls himself brahma-bandhu, “a brahmana in name only.”
  8. One of the biographies puts this comment at the beginning of its account of Vasudeva, without qualification, as if it concerned him. In the “Anubhashya” it belongs to Madhya 7.130 — to the order given to Kurma and the other householders; to Vasudeva the Lord gave His own, similar order (7.147–148).
  9. According to the biographies, in each other's arms they sang the glories of Mahaprabhu (one says they were immersed in prema) and wept in separation. In the “Charitamrita” they wept, remembering the Lord's qualities — that is, His mercy.
  10. These accounts differ both from the “Charitamrita” and from one another. Murari Gupta has neither the late arrival nor the swoon: Vasudeva sees the Lord and dances. In Lochana Dasa the Lord meets both brahmanas together, and leprosy is not mentioned. In the “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” the Lord Himself finds Vasudeva, and the healing follows Sudama's verse, whereas in the “Charitamrita” the verse is spoken after the healing. In the “Gaura-krishnodaya” Vasudeva does not lose consciousness but rolls on the ground weeping, and the Lord embraces him again and again. The instructions differ too: in the “Charitamrita” — to chant the name and instruct others, that is, to become an acharya; in Karnapura's mahakavya — “one free of selfishness will come to Me”; in the drama — “the mind will turn to nothing but the remembrance of the Lord”; in Murari Gupta and Lochana Dasa — both brahmanas are to spread devotion and sankirtana. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  11. “The Harmonist” places this meeting “in the temple of Kurma”; according to the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 7.138–140) and the “Anubhashya” (on 7.136) it took place at the house of the brahmana Kurma, in Kurma-kshetra.
